plan.title: 10 Surprising Facts About the Human Body
plan.description: Ten surprising facts about the human body, from bones that fuse to cells that renew constantly. Discover how your skeleton, blood and skin are more extraordinary than you think.

beats.narration: You started life with about 300 bones, but you have only 206 now. Where did the rest go? Your body is full of strange surprises, and here are ten.

props.label: Adult bones, down from about 300 at birth
props.delta: Some bones fuse as you g

beats.narration: Fact one: babies are born with roughly 300 bones, and as they grow, some fuse together. Fact two: more than half of your bones are in your hands, wrists, feet and ankles.

props.heading: Bones
items: Over half in hands and feet

beats.narration: Fact three: your body makes 25 million new cells every second. In just 15 seconds, you produce more cells than there are people in the United States.

props.label: new cells made by your body every second

beats.narration: Fact four: the largest bone is the femur, your thigh bone. The smallest is the stirrup, tucked inside your ear. Fact five: you are about one centimeter shorter at bedtime than when you woke up.
Fact six: your blood vessels stretch between 60,000 and 100,000 miles. Laid end to end, they would circle the world more than three times.

props.label: Minimum length of your blood vessels

beats.narration: Fact seven: a blood cell circles your whole body in about 60 seconds. It leaves the Heart, travels through the Body, and comes Back again, ready for another lap.
Fact eight: nerve impulses can travel as fast as 250 miles per hour. A signal from your toe reaches your brain before you can blink.
Fact nine: your skin cells live only two or three weeks, so you get a fresh coat every few weeks. You even lose about four kilograms of skin cells every year.
Fact ten: humans are the only species known to blush. So remember, your body is renewing, racing and surprising you every single second.

props.text: Humans are the only species known to blush.

hook_close.hook_text: You started life with about 300 bones, but you have only 206 now. Where did the rest go? Your body is full of strange surprises, and here are ten.
hook_close.close_text: Fact ten: humans are the only species known to blush. So remember, your body is renewing, racing and surprising you every single second.

accuracy.reason: Several claims are shaky: "about 300 bones" (the notes say 300 and 350), the nerve speed claim "before you can blink" is invented, and the "60,000 to 100,000 miles" vessel range is stated without hedging. The stirrup is described as "inside your ear", which is fine. The ear-bone pairing in the visual (femur 50 vs stirrup 1) is invented scale data.

coverage.reason: It has ten counted facts, but they cluster on bones (facts 1, 2 and 4), and facts 4 and 5 are crammed into one beat. Explanations are thin, and there is little on the brain, senses or microbiome.

structure.reason: The order is clear and the facts are numbered, but it is a flat list with weak transitions. The bone cluster up front feels repetitive, and the ending is hurried.

hook_ending.reason: The opening question about where the bones went is a decent hook. The ending is a generic summary line, "renewing, racing and surprising you", tacked onto fact ten.

tone.reason: Conversational and suited to a general audience, though somewhat flat.

visuals.reason: The scene types vary, but the scale_compare uses invented values (50 vs 1) that are not real data. The traffic light-trails clip is only loosely tied to nerve speed. The diagram uses capitalised labels awkwardly, and the narration reads them out: "Heart... Body... Back again".

originality.reason: The facts are the standard listicle fare (206 bones, blushing, shrinking at night). The 25 million cells versus US population comparison is the only slightly fresher touch.

instructions.reason: It delivers ten numbered facts in English at roughly the right length.

language.reason: The grammar is clean. The capitalised "Heart", "Body" and "Back again" in beat 6 read awkwardly.

defects.quote: A signal from your toe reaches your brain before you can blink.
defects.issue: This is an invented, unsupported claim. A blink takes about 100-150 ms, and a toe-to-brain signal at 250 mph takes roughly 20 ms, so it is plausible but not in the notes, and it is stated as fact.
The chart values are made up. The femur is about 48 cm and the stirrup about 0.3 cm, so the 1.0 value misrepresents the real ratio.

defects.quote: Fact four: the largest bone is the femur, your thigh bone. The smallest is the stirrup, tucked inside your ear. Fact five: you are about one centimeter shorter
defects.issue: Two facts are crammed into one beat, and the shrinking-at-night fact gets no visual or explanation.

defects.quote: babies are born with roughly 300 bones
defects.issue: The sources give both 300 and 350, and the script does not acknowledge the discrepancy.

defects.quote: Fact two: more than half of your bones are in your hands, wrists, feet and ankles.
defects.issue: Three of the ten facts are about bone counts or bone location, which makes the list repetitive. Fact one is also already spoken in the hook.

defects.quote: So remember, your body is renewing, racing and surprising you every single second.
defects.issue: This is a generic summary, tacked onto the final fact, and it does not leave a memorable image.

defects.quote: It leaves the Heart, travels through the Body, and comes Back again
defects.issue: Odd capitalisation, copied from the diagram labels, makes the narration read awkwardly.

missing: Brain or senses facts, such as a nose able to recognise a trillion scents
Microbiome facts, such as bacteria in the belly button
Explanations of why each fact is true
wrong_facts: Femur 50 vs stirrup 1 chart values are invented
"before you can blink" is unsupported by the notes
Bones at birth: sources vary between 300 and 350
judge.summary: A serviceable, correctly counted listicle with a decent opening hook, but it leans on bone facts, includes an invented chart and an unsupported claim, and ends with a generic wrap-up. It is acceptable but not publishable as is.
